Edward FitzGerald's Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám is an English verse translation and radical reinterpretation of a collection of Persian quatrains attributed to the medieval mathematician and poet Omar Khayyám. FitzGerald's free, poetic rendering wove together Persian verses into a unified narrative of wine, love, and mortality, and it became the dominant way English readers encountered Omar Khayyám, though it bears little resemblance to the original's fragmented nature.

FitzGerald published the work anonymously in eighteen fifty-nine and revised it five times over his lifetime, constantly tinkering and reordering the quatrains into an increasingly sophisticated whole. The original Persian Rubáiyát is a dispersed collection of independent four-line stanzas, often misattributed to Omar Khayyám. FitzGerald assembled them into a narrative arc about seizing pleasure before death. He rendered them in an interlocking rhyme scheme, AABA, in mellifluous English couplets quite unlike the tighter and more aphoristic original Farsi rubaí.

The work contains explicit hedonism—wine, love, sensory joy—and a cynicism about fate that scandalized some Victorian moralists, making the book daringly subversive for its time. FitzGerald's fame revived interest in Omar Khayyam across Europe, though modern scholars now argue that many stanzas may not be his at all and that FitzGerald invented more of the character than was present in the sources. The translation became iconic in late Victorian and Aesthetic movement culture, quoted and anthologized widely. Its opening, "Awake! for Morning in the Bowl of Night," remains its most famous passage. Later scholars and translators have offered more literal, scholarly versions, revealing the gap between FitzGerald's poetic liberty and philological accuracy.
